difficultyReason: The stimulus presents a mix of quantitative findings and a qualifying subgroup exception. The correct answer respects both the main trend and the qualification. Trap answers either drop the qualification (too strong) or over-apply the subgroup finding to the whole population (scope creep).
stimulus: A five-year study tracking 4,200 adults who regularly consumed fermented dairy products found that approximately 60 percent showed measurably lower markers of systemic inflammation compared to adults who consumed no fermented dairy. However, among participants who had previously been diagnosed with a specific autoimmune condition, those who consumed fermented dairy showed no significant difference in inflammation markers relative to those who did not. The study did not measure participants' overall diet quality or exercise frequency.
questionStem: The information above most strongly supports which one of the following claims?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Consuming fermented dairy products reduces systemic inflammation in all adults who do not have autoimmune conditions.

choices.label: B
choices.text: For at least some adults, regular consumption of fermented dairy products is associated with lower levels of systemic inflammation.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Diet quality and exercise frequency are the primary factors determining systemic inflammation levels in adults.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Adults with autoimmune conditions experience higher baseline levels of systemic inflammation than other adults.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Fermented dairy products are more effective at reducing inflammation than any other dietary intervention.

explanations.correct: The study found that roughly 60 percent of regular consumers of fermented dairy showed lower inflammation markers, which directly and strongly supports a hedged claim that for at least some adults, consumption is associated with lower inflammation. This respects the observational (correlational) nature of the data without overclaiming causation or universality.
explanations.A: Too strong — the stimulus establishes a majority finding among a study sample, not a universal rule. It also does not isolate autoimmune status as the only moderating variable, and the phrase 'all adults who do not have autoimmune conditions' goes far beyond what the data establish.
explanations.B: Correct. The 60 percent figure provides strong inductive support for the hedged claim that at least some adults show the association.
explanations.C: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus explicitly notes that diet quality and exercise were not measured, so no conclusion about their relative importance can be drawn from these data.
explanations.D: Opposite/scope creep — the study compared inflammation within each group (consumers vs. non-consumers), not between the autoimmune group and the general population. No baseline comparison across groups is reported.
explanations.E: Too strong and out of scope — the study makes no comparison to other dietary interventions whatsoever.

difficultyReason: The stimulus contains an economic trend alongside a counterintuitive exception for a specific sector. The correct answer draws a modest comparative inference. Traps include an absolute over-claim, a reversal of the direction of support, and a plausible economic truism not grounded in the stimulus.
stimulus: Data from a regional commerce bureau show that during the three years following a significant rise in interest rates, the number of new small-business registrations in the region declined by 22 percent. During the same period, new registrations in the home-repair and renovation sector increased by 14 percent. The bureau's report notes that many homeowners in the region chose not to sell their homes during the period of high rates, electing instead to invest in renovations.
questionStem: Which one of the following is most strongly supported by the information above?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Rising interest rates invariably cause a decline in new small-business registrations across all economic sectors.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The home-repair and renovation sector is unaffected by changes in interest rates.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Not all small-business sectors responded in the same way to the rise in interest rates in this region.

choices.label: D
choices.text: High interest rates ultimately benefit regional economies by redirecting consumer spending toward home improvement.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Homeowners who renovate rather than sell their homes generate more regional economic activity than homeowners who sell.

explanations.correct: The stimulus establishes two divergent sector-level outcomes during the same period: overall small-business registrations fell 22 percent while home-repair registrations rose 14 percent. This directly and strongly supports the claim that not all sectors responded identically — a straightforward comparative inference that does not require any step beyond the data.
explanations.A: Too strong — 'invariably' and 'all economic sectors' overreach. The data cover one region over one period, and the home-repair exception is explicitly presented in the stimulus.
explanations.B: Too strong and opposite in spirit — the sector did respond to higher rates (positively, via homeowner behavior), meaning it was not unaffected. The stimulus provides a causal mechanism linking rate changes to renovation activity.
explanations.C: Correct. The overall decline versus the sector-specific increase directly supports this modest comparative claim.
explanations.D: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus does not evaluate net regional economic benefit or compare the value of renovation spending to other forms of economic activity.
explanations.E: Out of scope — the stimulus provides no data comparing economic activity generated by renovating homeowners versus selling homeowners.

difficultyReason: The stimulus presents linguistic fieldwork data with a qualification about data collection conditions. The correct answer requires integrating the main finding with the qualifier. Distractors include an absolute over-claim, a plausible-but-unsupported linguistic generalization, and a mis-scoped inference that extends the finding beyond the study's population.
stimulus: Linguists conducting fieldwork among speakers of an endangered language in a mountainous region of Central Asia documented that speakers under the age of 35 used the language's traditional tonal distinctions inconsistently in casual conversation, while speakers over the age of 60 maintained those distinctions consistently. Speakers between the ages of 35 and 60 showed intermediate patterns. The fieldwork was conducted exclusively in village settings; no data were collected from speakers who had migrated to urban areas.
questionStem: The statements above, if true, most support which one of the following?

choices.label: A
choices.text: In at least some endangered languages, younger village-dwelling speakers tend to preserve tonal distinctions less consistently than older speakers do.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Tonal distinctions in endangered languages are always better preserved among rural populations than among urban populations.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The tonal distinctions of this language will be entirely absent from the speech of the next generation of speakers.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Urban migrants from this language community have abandoned tonal distinctions more thoroughly than village-dwelling speakers have.

choices.label: E
choices.text: Languages with tonal distinctions are more vulnerable to extinction than languages without such distinctions.

explanations.correct: The fieldwork data directly show that younger village-dwelling speakers used tonal distinctions inconsistently while older speakers maintained them consistently. The hedged phrasing 'in at least some endangered languages' and 'tend to' respects both the single-language scope of the study and the observational (rather than absolute) nature of the finding. This is the most defensible inference from the data.
explanations.A: Correct. The hedge 'at least some' limits the claim to what the one documented case licenses, and 'tend to' matches the probabilistic nature of the consistency data.
explanations.B: Too strong and out of scope — the study explicitly collected no data from urban speakers, so no rural-versus-urban comparison can be made. 'Always' is an extreme claim unsupported by data from a single language community.
explanations.C: Too strong — the data show inconsistent use, not complete absence, among younger speakers. Projecting total disappearance in the next generation goes well beyond what inconsistency patterns license.
explanations.D: Opposite/unsupported — the stimulus explicitly states no data were collected from urban migrants, so any claim about their speech patterns relative to village speakers is entirely unsupported.
explanations.E: Plausible but unsupported — the stimulus provides no comparative data about extinction rates of tonal versus non-tonal languages; it documents patterns within a single language.
